item.title: [World news | The Guardian] ‘I couldn’t breathe’: the deadly health burden of wildfire smoke
item.description:
Scientists race to untangle complex links between exposure and mortality as fire weather grows more prevalent

A thousand kilometres from the infernos gorging on northern Ontario’s boreal forests, Erin O’Connor watched the sky above Canada’s biggest city turn an “almost post-apocalyptic” orange as it filled with light-scattering particles of soot and ash. Stepping outside the halls of Toronto General hospital, where air filters were keeping patients safe from the worst of the fumes, she was struck by a smell so strong it felt like standing by a campfire.

“It really hit you in the face as soon as you walked outside,” said O’Connor, who runs University Health Network’s emergency department and saw a rise in patients presenting with allergies and shortness of breath. “As the days progressed, it was like that everywhere. It seemed even inside you could smell that burning.”

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Spanish mountain village braces for astrotourists lured by total solar eclipse
item.description:
Somosierra will be prime spot to view celestial alignment on 12 August, an event that poses logistical challenges

Little stirs in the mountains above Somosierra beyond the wind that lashes the flat peaks, the cows that graze on parched grass and the sun that beats down on the abandoned aerodrome where generations of glider pilots learned to ride air currents alongside squadrons of vultures and red kites.

But all this stillness will disappear, albeit temporarily, on the evening of 12 August, when swathes of northern and eastern Spain and the Balearic islands experience a total solar eclipse, the likes of which has not been seen here for more than 120 years.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Turkey and Saudi Arabia's rocky relations: A brief history
item.description:
Turkey and Saudi Arabia's rocky relations: A brief history

Submitted by Rayhan Uddin on Sat, 08/08/2026 - 14:44
As Riyadh and Ankara sign a historic defence agreement with Pakistan, MEE charts the turbulent ties between the two powers
Turkey’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is received by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, on 7 August 2026 (Saudi Press Agency/Handout via Reuters)
Off

In a highly symbolic move, the leaders of Saudi Arabia and Turkey were pictured performing Friday prayers together this week in the holy city of Mecca. 

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman were joined at the holiest site in Islam by Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.

For years, Ankara and Riyadh have been moving closer together and mending previously turbulent relations. 

That process was further solidified in recent days after Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a historic joint defence agreement. 

The agreement brings the three Muslim powers under a single security umbrella for the first time as part of a trilateral framework.

While Pakistan has maintained close ties with both countries for decades, Turkey and Saudi Arabia have not always seen eye to eye.

From historical rivalries over territory and religious sites to periods of cordial relations and a rupture over the killing of a journalist, Middle East Eye takes a brief look at the history of relations between the two countries.

Sunni Muslim powers 

There has long been low-level tension between Riyadh and Ankara over their competing claims to leadership of the Sunni Muslim world, dating back to the establishment of both states in the early 20th century.

The House of Saud fought the Ottoman Empire during the Ottoman-Saudi war in the 19th century, with the Saudis taking control of swathes of territory before a brutal crackdown by the Ottoman rulers.

After the fall of the Ottoman dynasty following the Arab revolt in 1916, the Saudis defeated local rivals and took control of the holy cities of Mecca and Medina by 1924. 

Footage: Saudi Crown Prince MbS, Erdogan and Sharif together perform Friday prayers in Mecca pic.twitter.com/tsVx6yV5Nt

— Ragıp Soylu (@ragipsoylu) August 7, 2026

The Ottomans had controlled Islam's two holiest sites almost continuously for more than 350 years.

The nascent states of Saudi Arabia and Turkey formally established relations in the 1930s, and the two countries remained cordial for many decades.

Both supported Iraq during the Iran-Iraq war, though Riyadh did so more openly, and both supported the US during the Gulf war. 

Tensions occasionally simmered over Islamic cultural heritage, with Turkey long criticising the demolition of Ottoman sites, including fortresses, cemeteries and railways, in Saudi Arabia.

In 2002, the Turkish culture ministry condemned the Saudi demolition of the then 220-year-old al-Ajyad fortress, which overlooks the Grand Mosque in Mecca. 

Murat Sokmenoglu, then Turkey’s parliament speaker, called it “sinful behaviour in breach of the moral values of Islam”. 

Riyadh defended the decision, stating that it was exercising its sovereignty and using the site to house pilgrims in Mecca. The Clock Tower in Mecca, one of the world’s tallest buildings, was later built where the fortress once stood. 

Arab Spring divergence

Cordial relations, punctuated by occasional minor disputes, gave way to much deeper disagreements following the Arab Spring in 2010.

Although both countries supported the overthrow of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in Syria, their wider approach to revolutionary movements in the region diverged. 

In Egypt, Turkey supported Mohamed Morsi - the first democratically elected president - and strongly opposed the 2013 military coup led by Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, a friend and ally of Riyadh. 

Following the coup, Turkey was welcoming of Egypt’s opposition, allowing dissenting media platforms to base themselves on Turkish soil. 

What Pakistan's defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey means for the Middle East
Read More »

For years, Erdogan refused to recognise Sisi’s rule and called for the release of 65,000 political prisoners. 

Ankara and Riyadh diverged in other arenas too. 

In 2017, when Saudi Arabia (alongside the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Egypt) imposed a blockade on Qatar, accusing it of meddling in regional countries and supporting terrorism, Turkey sided with Doha.

Meanwhile, in Libya, following the fragmentation of power after the 2011 revolution, Ankara supported the internationally recognised government in Tripoli, while Riyadh initially aligned itself with eastern-based warlord Khalifa Haftar.

A war of words between Riyadh and Ankara came to a head in early 2018, when Mohammed bin Salman said Turkey was part of a “triangle of evil” alongside Iran and extremist religious groups. 

Khashoggi killing

Ties between the two hit their lowest in modern times later that year following the killing of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi. 

Khashoggi, a former MEE journalist, was murdered by Saudi agents at the country's consulate in Istanbul in October 2018. 

Turkish prosecutors later indicted 20 Saudis over the killing, based on an analysis of the suspects’ mobile phone records, records of their entry into and exit from Turkey, their presence at the consulate, witness statements, and an examination of Khashoggi's phone, laptop and iPad.

Erdogan said the killing was ordered at the "highest levels" of the Saudi government.

Turkey’s state broadcaster and news agency were blocked in Saudi Arabia in 2010, and Ankara responded by blocking Saudi and Emirati news websites. 

Riyadh also launched an unofficial boycott of Turkish goods, causing Turkey’s exports to the Gulf kingdom to drop 92 percent year on year in 2021. 

The Saudi government had systematically pressured local businesses not to trade with Turkish companies and to drop their goods from their shelves.

Regional rapprochement 

The two countries ended their years-long rift in 2022 as part of a wider period of rapprochement in the region.

Mohammed bin Salman visited Ankara in June that year for the first time since Khashoggi’s killing. 

He met Erdogan at the presidential palace, where the two countries agreed to deepen cooperation on monetary policy, defence, energy and tourism.

Bab al-Mandeb: US war on Iran gives Houthis new leverage over Saudi Arabia
Read More »

The meeting came after a Turkish court transferred the Khashoggi murder case to Saudi Arabia, meeting a key demand from the Gulf kingdom for mending ties.

The reconciliation came amid a wider regional shift towards rapprochement led by the Saudi crown prince. 

That included ending the three and a half year rift with Qatar, seeking to engage with the Houthis in Yemen, as well as restoring diplomatic relations with Iran following a China-brokered agreement. 

At the same time, Ankara, for its part, restored fractured relations with Egypt and the UAE.

At a time when Turkey was dealing with a fragile economy and a massive slump in its currency, ending its rifts with oil-rich Gulf states was seen as key to economic stabilisation. 

Since patching up ties, Turkey and Saudi Arabia have signed deals on technology, defence and renewable energy. 

In the summer of 2023, Saudi Arabia agreed to buy Turkish drones in the biggest defence contract in Turkey's history.

Aligning goals

More recently, Turkey and Saudi Arabia appear to be coming closer together due to a shared understanding over events in neighbouring countries. 

In Syria, both Riyadh and Ankara support the new government led by Ahmed al-Sharaa and are among Damascus’ closest allies. 

Why are Kurdish groups in Iraq being attacked amid the US-Iran flare-up?
Read More »

Both countries were involved in lobbying for the US to lift sanctions on Syria. 

In Libya, while they had at times backed rival camps, they now both appear to support the internationally recognised government. 

Meanwhile in war-torn Sudan, Riyadh and Ankara both support the Sudanese Armed Forces, led by Abdel Fattah al-Burhan. 

The UAE is the main backer of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. 

Somalia is another arena where Turkey and Saudi Arabia find themselves on one side and Abu Dhabi on the other.

Ankara and Riyadh stand firmly behind the central government, while the UAE has steadily supported Somaliland’s efforts to gain international recognition.

Rather than Qatar or Turkey, it now seems that Saudi Arabia's growing rift is with its erstwhile Gulf ally, the UAE. That came to a head publicly for the first time in Yemen in late December.

Ankara appears increasingly aligned with Riyadh amid those tensions, although it is unlikely to take sides publicly because of its strong financial ties with Abu Dhabi.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] France shuts mosque over Quran verses and Islamic texts used in Muslim worship
item.description:
France shuts mosque over Quran verses and Islamic texts used in Muslim worship

Submitted by Elis Gjevori on Sat, 08/08/2026 - 17:53
A lawyer for the mosque says the six-month closure strikes at religious freedom and secularism in France
A French mounted police officer stand guard outside the Grande Mosquee or the Great Mosque during the Eid Al-Adha morning prayers, in Paris on June 28, 2023. (Zakaria Abdelkafi/AFP)
Off

A French court has upheld the six-month closure of a mosque near Paris in a case that has raised fresh concerns over the state’s policing of Islamic belief and worship.

The Montreuil Administrative Court on Friday rejected an attempt to suspend the July order against the Chanteloup mosque in Aulnay-sous-Bois. The mosque will remain closed until January.

Rafik Chekkat, a human rights lawyer representing the mosque, questioned whether imams in France remained free to recite Islam’s sacred text.

“In France, can an imam still quote the Quran in the mosque where he preaches?” said Chekkat.

Chekkat said the authorities based part of their case on imams “quoting...seven passages from the Quran and references to major works of the Islamic tradition, such as The Garden of the Righteous and The Forty Hadiths.”

The major works in question form part of the body of work of the 13th-century Syrian scholar Imam al-Nawawi, who is widely regarded as one of the Muslim world’s most important thinkers.

“We will file an appeal before the Council of State to defend religious freedom, freedom of expression, and the principle of secularism,” he added.

The authorities also objected to sermons “evoking ‘hell’ and the ‘punishments of the grave’ reserved for ‘unbelievers’”, despite similar teachings forming part of religious preaching in churches and other places of worship.

Eight out of 10 Muslims experience 'widespread' hatred in France, survey says
Read More »

Judges ruled that the prefect of Seine-Saint-Denis, Julien Charles, “did not commit a serious and manifestly illegal infringement of either the freedom of worship or the freedom of expression”.

“We are very disappointed by the decision and very surprised by its content. We will obviously go before the Council of State,” Chekkat told AFP, adding that parts of the ruling went “totally against religious freedom”.

“I understand that the administrative judge did not want to contradict the prefect of Seine-Saint-Denis, now I think that before the Council of State we will have a little more chance, it will be a little more legal and a little less political,” he said.

The decision follows years of expanding state pressure on Muslim institutions. French authorities closed 22 mosques in 18 months by April 2022, often using intelligence documents whose sources remained hidden.

The government has also dissolved Muslim organisations, including the Collective Against Islamophobia in France and the charity BarakaCity, deepening fears that France is using security laws to restrict Muslims’ freedom of belief.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] ‘Super El Niño’ could bring wet winter and flooding to western US, climate scientists warn
item.description:
Weather system tied to warming sea surface expected to intensify in fall and winter, persisting until early spring 2027

El Niño, a recurring climate phenomenon marked by above-average sea surface temperatures, when changes in wind patterns allow warmer water to spread across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, could spell a wet winter for portions of the western and south-eastern US, climate models show. Coastal areas may be at elevated risk of flooding, experts warn.

Climate scientists predict this year’s “super” El Niño, a label assigned when sea surface temperatures climb by at least 2C, will be the strongest of the century. The weather system is expected to intensify in the fall and winter, persisting until early spring 2027, according to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa).

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Three Palestinians killed and dozens wounded in Israeli attacks across Gaza and West Bank
item.description:
Three Palestinians killed and dozens wounded in Israeli attacks across Gaza and West Bank

Submitted by MEE staff on Sat, 08/08/2026 - 20:56
Jewish settlers opened fire and vandalised Palestinian property as Israeli forces raided homes, towns and a mosque across the West Bank
A mourner carries the shrouded body of an infant killed in an overnight Israeli airstrike the Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City on August 2, 2026. (Omar Al Qattaa/AFP)
Off

Three Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza, while Israeli forces and Jewish settlers wounded dozens more across the occupied West Bank on Saturday.

In the West Bank city of Tubas, Israeli forces stormed the city with military vehicles and deployed soldiers through the centre. The Palestinian Red Crescent Society treated 15 people after troops fired tear gas at residents.

Israeli forces also raided al Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah, and fired tear gas inside a house, leaving members of a family, including children, struggling to breathe.

Troops entered the nearby town of Turmus Ayya and the village of Abu Falah, while another Israeli force raided Kobar and fired tear gas in its streets.

Further south, Israeli settlers opened fire during an attack on Wadi al-Rakhim in Masafer Yatta, wounding four Palestinians. Medical workers took a 57-year-old man to hospital after a bullet struck his hand.

Settlers, operating under the protection of Israeli forces, also attacked the area surrounding the Prophet Saleh Mosque in Idhna, west of Hebron. They assaulted residents, fired live ammunition and erected a tent on privately owned Palestinian land.

'Used as human bait': Leaked image shows elderly Palestinian men before execution by Israeli forces
Read More »

Israeli soldiers entered the mosque during the settler assault and detained seven worshippers, including its imam, Mu’taz Sa’di Tmaizi.

Troops fired bullets, stun grenades and tear gas during the raid, while settlers vandalised a Palestinian vehicle.

Settlers also attacked Abu Falah and fired near the village school. Separate groups entered Beit Ur al-Tahta and roamed Palestinian farmland outside Jaljalia as Israeli forces provided protection.

The violence extended to Gaza, where Israeli troops shot three Palestinians in northern Khan Younis killing one. Nasser Medical Complex received the wounded.

Gaza’s Health Ministry said two more Palestinians had died from wounds sustained in previous Israeli attacks. Hospitals also received six wounded people, bringing the toll since the start of the genocide in October 2023 to 73,384 killed and 174,242 wounded.

Israel has killed 1,257 Palestinians and wounded 4,131 others since the October 2025 ceasefire took effect.

item.description:
Pentagon orders arms production surge as Israeli-US war on Iran depletes missiles

The Pentagon has ordered US arms manufacturers to accelerate weapons production as the Israeli-US war on Iran depletes American munition stockpiles.

In a memo obtained by The Washington Post, Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg gave defence companies 21 days to explain how they would “drive significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities”.

“Years-long development cycles are not acceptable,” Feinberg wrote. “We must dramatically accelerate our program schedules and expand our production capacity now.”

The order exposes the mounting strain the war has placed on US weapons reserves and follows tensions between President Donald Trump and Pentagon officials over dwindling missile supplies.

item.description:
'Used as human bait': Leaked image shows elderly Palestinian men before execution by Israeli forces

A newly leaked photograph shows two blindfolded elderly Palestinian men from Beit Lahia in Gaza, hours before Israeli forces killed them in November 2024, according to Palestinian journalist Younis Tirawi, who published the image.

The photograph shows Israeli military personnel standing between two blindfolded men, whom Tirawi identified in a post on X as Nadi Marouf and Ali Marouf.

He said the photograph was taken hours before their deaths and that the two men were "used as human bait and then executed".

In an earlier post in October 2025, Tirawi had said that troops from the 92nd Battalion of the Kfir Brigade abducted the men from Beit Lahia and held them as human shields for several days. 

"Israeli troops from the 92nd Battalion of the Kfir Brigade abducted two elderly Palestinians from Beit Lahia and used them as human shields for days before killing them," Tirawi wrote.

Citing the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, Wafa said the tender, published on 6 August 2026, has set 30 November 2026 as the deadline for development and construction companies to submit their bids.

The Kochav Yaakov settlement is built on the lands of the Ramallah and Al-Bireh Governorate.

The Commission said the housing project, covering 253.7 dunums (62.69 acres), has moved from planning to tendering stage in only 15 months.

During the first half of 2026, the Commission monitored the publication of 12 tenders by Israeli authorities, including 1,138 housing units in five main settlements, according to Wafa.

Some of these tenders, rather than focusing solely on residential expansion, are aimed at developing industrial and commercial zones, offices, nursing homes, and tourism and recreational facilities.

Vance says talks 'make progress' but Iran must make long-term changes

US vice president JD Vance has said the US has made progress in negotiations with Iran, but Washington remains focused on determining whether Tehran “is willing to make longer-term changes that could lead to an improved relationship with Washington”. 

“The question is whether they're able, their system is able to give the things that are necessary for us to be happy, for us to feel like we've gotten what we need out of this particular engagement. That is still to be determined, but I do think that we've made some progress over the last few days,” Vance told Fox News.

Vance reiterated that the US has “destroyed Iran’s nuclear programme, their conventional military and radically reduced their asymmetric military abilities”. 

“And right now we’re trying to see if they’re willing to make the kind of long-term changes that would be necessary to have a better relationship with the United States,” he said.

“And if not, that’s fine too. We’re just going to keep on applying the pressure that we can apply and getting as much oil and gas out of the Middle East so that Americans can enjoy lower gas and energy prices,” he added.

item.description:

Israeli troops infiltrated a Lebanese village placed under the control of Lebanon's army as part of a June agreement, building an earthen barrier there overnight.

An AFP correspondent saw the barrier, situated at the village's eastern entrance and blocking the road. The local authorities said it was unclear if any Israeli forces remained in the area.

"An Israeli occupation army force advanced into the village of Zawtar al-Gharbiya shortly after midnight... and erected a new earthen barrier near the town square," Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) reported.

Zawtar al-Gharbiya was one of two designated "pilot zones" where the Lebanese army was to take over as part of a US-sponsored framework agreement signed with Israel.

Contacted by AFP, the Israeli military said it was "not aware of such an event in this area".

Israeli forces continue to occupy a broad band of territory in the south along the border. Its invasion and widespread bombing campaign have killed more than 4,300 people and displaced hundreds of thousands more. (Reporting by AFP)

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Pakistani defence minister calls for 'united military front' against Israel
item.description:
Pakistani defence minister calls for 'united military front' against Israel

Pakistan’s defence minister Khawaja Asif has called for a “united military front” against Israel, calling it “a threat to the entire Muslim world”.

In an interview with Pakistan’s Geo News, after the country signed a landmark defence agreement with Turkey and Saudi Arabia, Asif said: “Given Israel’s current conduct, as well as the historical evidence of what it has been doing, at one stage, in 1948 or 1947, what I consider an illegitimate state came into being. It was, I believe, a product of the Balfour Declaration.”

“During that period as well, fighting continued and the Palestinians continued to resist. So, in my view, this is at the very least a situation that the entire Islamic world will have to come together and confront.”

“In my view, there is no room for disagreement on this. Until the issue of the Palestinian people is resolved according to their aspirations, the issue will remain,” he added.

He said the “anti-Palestinian and anti-Islamic nature” of the Israeli state "would not change, irrespective of who comes to power" and "they will continue to play off one Muslim nation against another".
